post.description:
OAuth2 compatible token login.

Authenticate with email and password to receive an access token and refresh token.

- **username**: User's email address (named 'username' for OAuth2 compatibility)
- **password**: User's password

Returns a JSON object with three fields:
- **access_token**: Short-lived JWT for authenticating API requests
- **refresh_token**: Long-lived opaque token for obtaining new access tokens
  without re-authenticating (via the `/login/refresh-token` endpoint)
- **token_type**: Always `"bearer"`

Note: This response shape differs from a standard OAuth2 token response by including
the `refresh_token` field alongside the `access_token`.

Refresh access token using a valid refresh token.

Exchange a valid refresh token for a new access token and refresh token pair.
No authentication header required.

**Token Rotation**: Each refresh token can only be used once. After use, the old
refresh token is invalidated and a new one is returned. This provides security
against token theft.

**Reuse Detection**: If a previously used refresh token is submitted, all refresh
tokens for the user are revoked as a security measure.

Logout by revoking the provided refresh token.

Requires a valid access token. This endpoint invalidates the given refresh token
so it can no longer be used to obtain new access tokens. The operation is
idempotent — calling it with an already-revoked or non-existent token will still
return 204.

Clients should also discard the access token locally after calling this endpoint.

Logout from all sessions by revoking all refresh tokens for the current user.

Requires a valid access token. After calling this endpoint, all existing refresh
tokens for the user are invalidated. Clients should also discard any locally
stored access tokens.

Refresh the list of models available from a language model provider.

Calls the provider's API using the credentials already stored for it — no
credentials are sent with this request. Models that are still offered keep
their `status`, models the provider no longer offers are dropped, and newly
offered ones appear enabled. A successful refresh also updates
`verified_at`.

be reached or rejects them, or when it answers with no models while models
are already stored; nothing is overwritten in those cases. A provider with
no models stored yet is allowed to answer with none, leaving it with an
empty model set.

is in flight, since the models fetched belong to the superseded ones.

environment through `POST /admin/organisation/import`. It is safe to read
and to copy: it contains **no credentials** — no language model provider
keys, no MCP authentication, no password hashes and no webhook tokens.

`manual_followup`.

Nothing is addressed by database id. Users are matched by e-mail, providers,
MCP servers and agents by their identifier slug, and knowledge-base folders
by their name-path, so the target environment assigns its own ids.

Which agents come across must be stated: `include_all_agents=true` for a
whole-tenant migration, or `agent_ids` to name a selection. With neither,
no agents are exported. A composite agent named in `agent_ids` is a 400,
while one met by `include_all_agents` is skipped and reported under

claim that every agent in it can be expressed in the DSL.

Create an organisation from an export document (platform admin only).

Accepts the YAML produced by `GET /admin/organisation/{id}/export`. The
organisation is created through the ordinary creation path, so it gets the
platform's baseline provisioning, and its own configuration is then applied
from the manifest the document carries — **synchronously, inside this
request**, not by a background task. By the time the response arrives the
providers, MCP servers, knowledge base and agents either exist or are named
in `warnings`, and `provisioning_applied` says which. A large knowledge base
therefore makes for a slow request.

password nobody knows. No e-mail is sent by this endpoint. Activating the
organisation is a separate call, and that is what sends each member their
activation link — so check the imported configuration first.

Two things must be done by hand afterwards, because the document never
carries a secret: language model provider credentials, and the
authentication of any MCP server listed under `manual_followup`. Set the
organisation's default model and embedding model once those providers are
verified. Knowledge-base documents arrive as **drafts** and are published
separately, once an embedding model is configured.

nothing and so creates no resource; a dry run also reports
`organisation_id: null`.

schema version from a newer release, a malformed e-mail address, an owner
missing from the users list, an e-mail address that is already taken, an
invalid credit allowance plan, a provider identifier claimed both as the
organisation's own and as a system grant, or a provider the document's
agents reference and this environment can neither create nor grant. The
import creates a new organisation and never merges into an existing one, so
a single colliding address refuses the whole file; the message names every
address that clashed, not just the first.

in the document references, is reported in `warnings` rather than refused —
an unused grant is not a reason to block a migration.

The agent answers in prose unless ``response_format`` asks otherwise, as on

Emits ``start``, then any of ``token`` / ``tool_call_start`` /
``tool_call_end`` / ``tool_call_error`` / ``mcp_auth_required`` /
``message`` events during the run, then ``done`` once the message has
been persisted. ``done`` carries ``message_id`` — the real, DB-assigned id
of the assistant's reply, for use with ``POST .../fork`` — unlike the
``message_id`` on each ``message`` frame, which is LangChain's own id,
assigned before that row exists. ``mcp_auth_required`` always accompanies
(never replaces) a ``tool_call_error`` for the same call — it signals
specifically that the failing tool's MCP server needs a per-user
connection that doesn't exist yet, and carries ``mcp_connect_url`` — the
frontend URL the user opens to establish it. Errors raised after the
stream is opened are delivered in-band as ``event: error`` — the HTTP
response itself stays 200. An organisation out of credits is refused that
way too, with code ``insufficient_credits``, before the agent runs. A turn
that runs past its time limit ends with code ``timeout``. When the server
has no stream capacity left, the stream ends with code ``streaming_busy``
and no ``id``, so the cursor is kept: reconnect with a ``GET`` to resume.

The first ``message`` frame is **the caller's own message**, echoed back with
``role: "user"`` before the agent produces anything. It is there because a run
is read by more than its sender — a second viewer, or the sender itself after a
reconnect — and without it a run carries an answer with no visible prompt. A
client that renders every ``message`` frame will therefore see the message it
just sent: fold it into whatever was rendered optimistically rather than
appending it twice. Its ``message_id`` is empty, unlike every other
``message`` frame: LangChain assigns one only when the turn is persisted, which
has not happened yet, and an invented id would match nothing later. Match it on
its content, which the sender knows because it just sent it.

Every frame carries an ``id`` naming this run and the frame's position in it,
*except* the terminal ``done``/``error``, which carry an empty ``id`` to reset
the client's cursor — nothing follows them in this run, so a reconnect should
ask for whatever is live rather than resume a run that has ended.

The run is published to Redis by a task that outlives this request, and this
response is simply the first subscriber to it — so losing this connection no
longer aborts the run, and the client resumes with a ``GET`` on this same path,
passing that id back as ``Last-Event-ID``. Any number of other viewers can
watch the same run at once.

only watches whichever run is current. So it never consumes credits, cannot be
refused with ``locked``, needs only read access, and any number of clients may
call it at once — a second browser tab, or the same client resuming after a
dropped connection.

Send ``Last-Event-ID`` to resume. The id names both the run and the position
within it, so a resume carries on with the run it was watching — through to
its ``done``, even if that run has finished in the meantime and the
conversation has moved on. That is what lets a client keep *appending* streamed
frames after a dropped connection rather than replacing the turn wholesale. An
id this API did not issue is ignored, and the live run served instead.

Omit it — a second tab, a fresh page — and the response follows whichever run
is live, from its first frame.

client that reconnects after one is served the live run rather than the finished
one it was watching: the conversation is shared, and the turn that comes next
may be somebody else's. That is what stops an auto-reconnecting client from
pinning itself to a dead run.

cursor, or a cursor whose run has expired — the single frame
``event: no_active_run`` is returned and the response ends, so a client needs
no status-code handling to tell that apart from any other outcome. Fall back to
``GET .../messages/`` there: a run's message is persisted before its ``done``
frame, so by then the result is already readable.

When the server has no stream capacity left, the stream ends with an
``error`` frame with code ``streaming_busy`` and no ``id``, so the cursor is
kept: reconnect to resume.

`credits_min`/`credits_max`, `search` and `daterange`. Filters compose as AND: when several
are supplied, the result set is the intersection.
* If `agent_id` is provided, only executions of that agent will be returned.
* If one or more `status` values are provided, only executions with those statuses will be returned.
* If one or more `id` values are provided, only executions with those execution IDs will be
  returned; IDs outside the caller's organisation (or, for members, outside their own
  executions) are silently skipped rather than reported as missing.
* If one or more `created_by` user IDs are provided, only executions created by those users
  will be returned. This narrows what the caller may already see, it never widens it: a member
  is always restricted to their own executions, so filtering by anyone else returns an empty
  list.
* If one or more `trigger_definition_id` values are provided, only executions started by those
  trigger definitions will be returned. These are definition IDs — the kind of trigger, as
  listed by `GET /triggers/definitions` — not the IDs of individual triggers bound to an agent,
  so filtering by the scheduler's daily definition returns the runs of every daily schedule.
  Only runs that recorded an origin can match, so an execution with no trigger behind it is
  never returned by any value of this filter: that covers executions created before the
  platform began recording the origin, and the runs of the organisation's own system agents,
  which the platform starts directly rather than through a trigger.
* If one or more `trigger_type` values are provided, only executions whose trigger
  provenance buckets into one of those types are returned (see `TriggerType`).
* If `duration_min`/`duration_max` are provided, only executions whose duration (seconds)
  falls within that range are returned; executions with no recorded duration never match.
* If `credits_min`/`credits_max` are provided, only executions whose total consumed
  credits fall within that range are returned; executions with no recorded credit spend
  never match.
* If `search` is provided, only executions whose ID contains it as a substring are returned.
* If `daterange` is provided (e.g. `2026-01-01,2026-12-31`, `2026-01-01,` or `,2026-12-31`),
  only executions started within that range are returned; executions that have not started
  yet never match. Results are then ordered by start time, newest first.
* Without `daterange`, results are ordered by creation time, newest first.
* If no filter is provided, all executions available to the user will be returned (subject to
  pagination).

get.description:
Watch an agent execution as it runs.

Emits `queued` while the execution is still waiting for a worker, then
`started` once one has taken it and created its conversation, then the
agent's own frames — any of `token` / `tool_call_start` / `tool_call_end` /
`tool_call_error` / `mcp_auth_required` / `message` — and finally `done`,
carrying the terminal `status`, the `result` and the `response_format` it is
in. So a client learns the outcome from the stream itself and needs no
follow-up request.

Read-only, and deliberately weaker than triggering one: watching a run must
not require the right to start one. It consumes no credits, starts nothing,
and any number of clients may call it at once — a second browser tab, or the
same client resuming after a dropped connection.

Send `Last-Event-ID` to resume. Every frame except the terminal one carries
an `id` naming its position, and a reconnect carries on from the frame after
it — no duplicate, no gap — through to `done`. That is what lets a client keep
*appending* streamed output after a dropped connection rather than starting
the run's output over. An id this API did not issue is ignored and the run
replayed from its start.

The terminal `done` (and any `error`) carries an *empty* `id`, which resets the
client's cursor: nothing follows it, so an auto-reconnecting client comes back
without one instead of pinning itself to a run that has ended.

Always `200`. When there is nothing to serve — the run finished long enough ago
that its stream has expired, or no worker picked it up while this connection
waited — the single frame `event: no_active_run` is returned and the response
ends, so a client needs no status-code handling to tell that apart from any
other outcome. Fall back to `GET /executions/{execution_id}` there: the row is
committed before the terminal frame is published, so by then the status and
result are already readable.

When the server has no stream capacity left, the stream ends with an `error`
frame with code `streaming_busy` and no `id`, so the cursor is kept:
reconnect to resume.

post.description:
Cancel a running or queued agent execution.

Revokes the background task and stops the execution as `CANCELED`. A run that
has not started yet never runs and costs nothing.

A run already under way is asked to stop rather than killed, and stops at the
next step of the agent — so the response returns immediately while the worker
is still winding the run down. The outcome is discarded and the execution stays
`CANCELED`. Everything it consumed up to that point is charged: its tokens and
tool calls, its wall-clock, and the per-run fee.

Only org admins/owners or the execution creator may cancel, and only within
their own organisation. An execution that already reached `SUCCESS`,
`FAILURE` or `CANCELED` is refused with 400.

even if the trigger has been reconfigured since — retrying asks for the run

get.description:
List the caller organisation's credit history, newest first.

The unaggregated history behind every other figure here: one LEDGER row per
credit movement — purchases and adjustments as well as the one or two debits
each consumption is split into by funding source — interleaved with a
PLAN_CHANGE row for each change to the monthly allowance cap. Ordered by
`occurred_at` descending, then by `entry_type` and `id` descending so rows
sharing an instant page consistently. The ledger is append-only, so an entry
never changes once written; its `execution` status is read live.

Each row carries `balance_after` (total balance, allowance remaining plus
purchased, right after it was recorded) and `ordered_by` (the agent for an
agent run, otherwise the user, with their avatar). A consumption also
carries its `execution` (status and duration). A plan change is listed once
it takes effect; a change still scheduled for later does not appear yet.

Amounts are gross and nothing is netted: a reversal appears as its own entry
alongside the consumption it reverses, rather than reducing it. `amount` is
always positive — `direction` carries the sign.

Paginated via `skip`/`limit`, with `total_count` set to the number of
matching rows. Filters compose: when several are supplied the result is
their intersection. Filtering by `agent_id`, `user_id`, `execution_id`, or
`conversation_id` matches on what a consumption was attributed to, so it
necessarily excludes purchases and manual adjustments — those carry no
attribution at all. Any of those, `direction`, or `category` also excludes
plan changes; `entry_type` keeps one kind of row only.

Requires an organisation owner or admin: an entry names the user and agent
that spent the credits, the same management information `GET /credits/usage`
exposes. A member reading their own spend uses `GET /credits/usage/me`.

get.description:
Return the caller's own daily spend over a range, plus derived stats.

Every day in the range is present, ascending; a day with no consumption is
reported as zero rather than omitted. `avg_daily_spend` divides the total by
every day in the range, zero days included, and `most_expensive_day` is the
single highest-spend day (ties go to the earliest), or null when the whole
range spent nothing.

`comparison` compares the requested range to an equally long window right
before it — pass a week-long `daterange` for a "this week vs last week"
view — the same `PRECEDING_PERIOD` shape as the organisation-wide `GET
/credits/usage/comparison`, fixed rather than a `compare_to` choice: a
personal view has no monthly allowance to compare a calendar month against.
`top_agent` is the single agent the caller spent the most on in the range,
or null when nothing in it is attributed to an agent.

Both ends of `daterange` are required, the end may not precede the start,
and the range may not span more than a year. No id is accepted: the caller
always reads their own usage. For any other member's usage, or a breakdown
by agent/user/execution, see `GET /credits/usage` (owner/admin).

Readable by any organisation member.

The earlier window is derived by the server, not requested. `compare_to` picks
the rule and is echoed back: `PREVIOUS_MONTH` (the default) is the whole
calendar month before the month the range starts in, and `PRECEDING_PERIOD` is
the equally long window ending the day before the range starts. Both windows
come back with their bounds, their day count, and their allowance/purchased
split.

The two windows are not necessarily the same length — a month-to-date range
against a whole previous month is the common case — so `change` and
`change_ratio` compare totals, not daily rates. Divide each window's
`credits_spent` by its `days` before presenting a trend.

The range is used exactly as given: days that have not happened yet are
included as zero and lower `current` accordingly. Both ends of `daterange` are
required, and the end may not precede the start.

with no per-agent or per-user breakdown. For that breakdown use `GET
/credits/usage`, which requires an owner or admin.

get.description:
Return the caller organisation's currently-effective allowance plan.

Scoped to the caller's own organisation (never another org's) — the service
derives the organisation from the authenticated user, so the route supplies no
id. Requires an organisation owner or admin. Setting a plan is a platform
action and lives on the ``/admin/credits`` router. Returns 404 when no plan is
currently in effect.

404.description: No allowance plan configured for the organisation

post.description:
Open a new allowance plan for an organisation (superuser only).

Plans are append-only and effective-dated: this creates a new plan version,
closing the organisation's current open plan and opening the new one
effective from ``effective_from`` (or now). An existing plan is never mutated
in place — it is superseded. The monthly allowance is a computed cap, not
stored credits.

POST, not PUT: each call creates a distinct plan, so it is not idempotent.
Supplying the same explicit ``effective_from`` as the current open plan is
rejected with 400 (a new plan must start strictly after it); omitting it
opens another plan starting now. Do not blindly retry.

The 201 body is the created plan. Plans carry no surfaced id and are not
addressable individually — they are identified by their effective window — so
no ``Location`` header is returned; read the effective plan via
``GET .../allowance-plans/current``.

Grant an organisation extra credits (superuser only).

Extra credits are stored and never expire: they are spent only once the
organisation's monthly allowance is used up. The response is the
organisation's updated balance.

Not idempotent: every call grants ``amount`` again, so do not blindly retry.

400.description: Invalid amount, or amount would take the purchased balance past its maximum

404.description: Resource not found or user has no permission to access it

post.description:
Revoke an organisation's extra credits (superuser only).

Draws only from the stored (purchased) credits; the monthly allowance is never
touched. An ``amount`` greater than the purchased balance is rejected with 400
rather than driving it negative. The response is the organisation's updated
balance.

Not idempotent: every call revokes ``amount`` again, so do not blindly retry.

404.description: Resource not found or user has no permission to access it

get.summary: Admin List Organisations By Budget Risk
get.description:
Return the organisations closest to running out of usable credits.

Candidates are every organisation with an active allowance plan,
platform-wide, ranked ascending by total remaining credits (allowance
remaining plus purchased) by default — the most at-risk organisation
first; pass `sort_by=status` to rank by status severity instead, or
`sort_by=percent_used` to rank descending by percentage of the monthly
allowance consumed. Paginated over that ranking with `skip`/`limit`
(default page size 6); `total_count` is the full candidate pool size, not
just the returned page — or, when `low_budget=true`, the size of the
filtered (non-OK) pool.

Each organisation's `status` (no budget / running out / OK) is derived
from its balance against the platform's warning threshold, so it's
available for every candidate regardless of pagination. Pass
`low_budget=true` to return only `running_out`/`no_budget` organisations.
`percent_used` is a separate, allowance-only metric (ignores purchased
credits) kept distinct from `status`/`credits_available` because it
mirrors an existing client-side calculation rather than a new definition.

`budget_forecast` is always about the current month through month end,
computed live at request time — it does not depend on any date range.
It projects *total* spend (allowance and purchased combined) against what
the organisation can still spend, never against `monthly_allowance`
alone: exhausting the allowance just shifts further spend onto the
purchased pool by design and is not itself a problem. Unlike `status`/
`percent_used`, it's only computed for the rows actually returned — as is
`usage_trend`, the same current-month day series `budget_forecast` is
derived from, included so a trend can be rendered without a second,
per-organisation forecast request.

`billing_period_end_date`/`days_until_billing_period_end` report each
organisation's own allowance-plan cycle boundary, not a forecast.

Superuser only.

Return platform-wide AGENT_EXECUTION spend statistics, broken down by
unit of work: triggered executions and plain conversation turns.

`execution` and `conversation` are independent breakdowns, not a mutually
exclusive split — a triggered execution running inside a conversation
contributes to both, so they do not sum to the platform's actual total
spend when they overlap. `total` does not have this overlap: its unit is
the execution or conversation itself (the same granularity `execution`/

exactly once there regardless of which of execution_id/conversation_id it
also carries.

`max_credits` is computed over that breakdown's own credits spent (summed
per unit first, then aggregated across units), across every organisation.

ContextWindowStrategy.title: ContextWindowStrategy
ContextWindowStrategy.description:
How an agent behaves when its conversation approaches the model's context window.

The default is `STOP` (today's behavior): the run simply fails once the
provider rejects an over-length request. The other two values opt into one
of LangChain's built-in middlewares that keep a long conversation going —
`CONTEXT_EDITING` clears old tool results, `SUMMARIZATION` replaces older
messages with an LLM-generated summary. Callers branch on `is_stop` /
`is_context_editing` / `is_summarization`, never on comparing the raw value.

CreditCategory.title: CreditCategory
CreditCategory.description:
Why a ledger row exists.

CREDIT rows use `PURCHASE`/`MANUAL_ADJUSTMENT`; DEBIT rows use the
consumption/adjustment reasons. The direction constrains which categories
are meaningful, but the enum lists them all in one place.

`SETTLEMENT` is an ALLOWANCE-funded DEBIT written at the start of a period
to pay a negative purchased pool off from the new allowance: it moves
credits from the allowance into the pool, so the total balance is unchanged.

CreditCurrency.title: CreditCurrency
CreditCurrency.description:
The unit a ledger amount is denominated in.

Always `CREDITS` for now — modelled as an enum (not a bare string) so
pricing and balance components import a typed member and the set of valid
currency has a single source of truth.

The value is intentionally lowercase (`"credits"`): unlike the
classification enums it is the currency token persisted on every row, and
lowercase is the form used across the schema and stored data.

type.description: AGENT for a consumption charged to an agent execution; USER for everything else (chat usage, purchases, adjustments, plan changes).

name.title: Name
name.description: The agent's name, or the user's full name falling back to their email.

agent_id.title: Agent Id
agent_id.description: Set when `type` is AGENT, unless the agent has since been deleted — then `name` is null too.

avatar_url.title: Avatar Url
avatar_url.description: The user's avatar. Always null for an agent, or for a user without one.

CreditEntryType.title: CreditEntryType
CreditEntryType.description:
What one row of the credit history listing is.

The listing interleaves two kinds of record that both move what an
organisation can spend: ledger rows (credits in, debits out) and allowance
plan changes (the monthly cap being raised or lowered). They live in
different tables with independent ids, so internally the pair
(`entry_type`, `id`) — not `id` alone — identifies a row. The API exposes
the id of ledger rows only; a plan change's id is internal.

CreditExecutionUsagePeriodSchema.title: CreditExecutionUsagePeriodSchema
CreditExecutionUsagePeriodSchema.description:
Credits spent on AGENT_EXECUTION consumption for a single time period.

Credits carry no currency, so unlike `AgentUsagePeriodSchema`/
`OrgUsagePeriodSchema` (which may have multiple rows per period, one per
currency) this is always at most one row per period.

`execution_credits_spent` and `conversation_credits_spent` are independent
sums (rows attributed to an execution, and rows attributed to a
conversation, respectively) — not a mutually exclusive split of
`credits_spent`. A triggered execution running inside a conversation counts
toward both, so the two do not in general add up to `credits_spent`.

CreditForecastDaySchema.title: CreditForecastDaySchema

model_identifier.title: Model Identifier
model_identifier.description: The model this consumption was recorded against, e.g. 'openai/gpt-4o'. Null for rows recorded before this dimension existed, or for non-model spend (e.g. execution wall-clock).

CreditLedgerEntryAttributionSchema.title: CreditLedgerEntryAttributionSchema
CreditLedgerEntryAttributionSchema.description:
What one consumption was recorded against.

Every dimension is nullable: a consumption need not name any of them. Foreign-keyed
dimensions are set to null when their target is deleted, while the ledger spend
row remains immutable.

status.description: The execution's current status — read live, so a run still in progress when it was charged shows its latest state.

duration.title: Duration
duration.description: Execution duration in seconds. Null until the run finishes.

CreditLedgerEntryExecutionSchema.title: CreditLedgerEntryExecutionSchema
CreditLedgerEntryExecutionSchema.description: The execution a consumption was charged for, as it stands now.

entry_type.description: LEDGER for a credit movement, PLAN_CHANGE for a change to the monthly allowance cap.

id.title: Id
id.description: The ledger entry's id. Null on a PLAN_CHANGE row.

direction.description: The sign of this row: CREDIT adds credits, DEBIT spends them. Each row stands alone — a DEBIT is not balanced by a second row. Null on a PLAN_CHANGE row, which moves no credits.

category.description: Why the row exists. SETTLEMENT marks the start-of-period payoff of negative extra credits from the new monthly allowance: an ALLOWANCE-funded DEBIT that brings the purchased credits back up by the same amount, leaving the total balance unchanged. Null on a PLAN_CHANGE row.

funding_source.description: Which pool a DEBIT drew from — ALLOWANCE (the monthly entitlement) or PURCHASE (stored credits). Always ALLOWANCE on a SETTLEMENT row. Always null on a CREDIT row, where it does not apply, and on a PLAN_CHANGE row.

amount.title: Amount
amount.description: Always positive: `direction` carries the sign, not the amount. Null on a PLAN_CHANGE row — its figures are in `plan_change`.

occurred_at.title: Occurred At
occurred_at.description: When the credits moved — the business time the row is dated by. For a PLAN_CHANGE row, when the new cap takes effect.

created_at.title: Created At
created_at.description: When the row was written. Later than `occurred_at` for a backdated entry.

balance_after.title: Balance After
balance_after.description: The organisation's total balance (allowance remaining plus purchased) immediately after this row was recorded. For a PLAN_CHANGE row, the balance as the new cap took effect.

ordered_by.description: Who to show the row as ordered by: the agent for an agent execution, otherwise the user. Null when there is no one to name — including platform staff outside the organisation who recorded a purchase or set a plan.

attribution.description: What the consumption was recorded against. Null for purchases, manual adjustments, settlements, and plan changes, which are organisation-level movements with no agent, user, execution, or conversation behind them.

execution.description: The execution the consumption was charged for, with its status and duration. Null when the row names no execution or it was deleted.

plan_change.description: The plan change itself. Set on PLAN_CHANGE rows only.

effective_to.title: Effective To
effective_to.description: When a later plan superseded this one. Null while it is current.

CreditPlanChangeSchema.title: CreditPlanChangeSchema
CreditPlanChangeSchema.description: The allowance plan change a PLAN_CHANGE row records.

previous.description: The earlier window, derived by the server from `compare_to` — not a range the caller supplies. It may be longer than `current`.

compare_to.description: The rule that produced `previous`, echoed back.

change.title: Change
change.description: `current.credits_spent` minus `previous.credits_spent`. A difference of totals, not of daily rates: with `compare_to=PREVIOUS_MONTH` an in-progress month is compared against a complete one, so this is negative for most of the month. Normalise by each window's `days` before showing a trend.

change_ratio.title: Change Ratio
change_ratio.description: `change` as a fraction of the previous window's total (0.2 is a 20% rise). Null when the previous window had no spend at all: growth from zero has no ratio — show `change` instead. Same totals-not-rates caveat as `change`.

DocumentParseStatus.title: DocumentParseStatus
DocumentParseStatus.description:
Lifecycle of a file-uploaded document's Markdown conversion.

Inline-authored documents are `COMPLETED` on creation (nothing to parse).
A file upload starts `PENDING`, moves to `PROCESSING` when the background
task picks it up, then to a terminal `COMPLETED` or `FAILED`.

DroppedTrigger.title: DroppedTrigger
DroppedTrigger.description:
A trigger that was deliberately not carried across.

Only the manual run-now trigger is exported, because every agent needs one
to be runnable. Scheduled triggers would start firing in the target the
moment the organisation goes live, and webhook triggers carry a secret
token — so both are recorded here and re-created by hand if still wanted.

EffectivePolicySchema.title: EffectivePolicySchema
EffectivePolicySchema.description: What actually applies, once the platform floor is folded in.

EmbeddingStatus.title: EmbeddingStatus
EmbeddingStatus.description:
Progress of embedding a version's chunks under the org's current model.

Informational only: retrieval never depends on it (search joins the actual
embedding rows, so an unembedded version simply yields no hits). `PENDING`
until a publish embeds the version, `READY` once every chunk is embedded,
`FAILED` if embedding gave up (the version then reverts to draft).

EntryDirection.title: EntryDirection
EntryDirection.description:
The sign of a single ledger row.

`direction` is the sign of the one row it sits on, not a second balancing
row — a CREDIT adds stored credits, a DEBIT spends them.

available metrics are relevant to this agent.

threshold.title: Threshold
threshold.description: The value this metric must reach to pass, in the metric's own unit/scale (e.g. 80.0 for an 80% success_rate, 5.0 for a 5-second latency cap, 0.7 for a 0.0-1.0 correctness score). Check GET /metric-providers/types for this metric_id's `unit` and `is_maximized` before choosing a threshold.

weight.title: Weight
weight.description: This metric's contribution to the overall quality score.

config.description: Metric-specific settings, e.g. a custom rubric or expected-tools list.

is_gate.title: Is Gate

the knowledge-base tools to an agent never silently grants the whole KB.
Whole-KB access is a positive, named value (`ALL`) — never the absence of a

MemoryConfidence.description:
Did the user say this, or did the agent conclude it.

A provenance question a model can answer reliably, unlike a confidence
score - a model that has just inferred something reports high confidence
as readily as it would for something stated outright. `INFERRED` selects
the short TTL and starts an entry as `CANDIDATE` rather than `ACTIVE`.
`DERIVED` is consolidation's output (2B) - summarised from several
sources, neither stated by the user nor a single-shot guess.

MemoryEntryListResponseSchema.title: MemoryEntryListResponseSchema

The DTO keeps `items` and `total` - those are the domain's words, and
this mapping is the boundary that lets each side name things its own

MemoryLifecycle.title: MemoryLifecycle
MemoryLifecycle.description:
Where an entry is in its life, which decides whether an agent sees it.

`CANDIDATE` is written once, not yet corroborated by a second observation.
Past its own `expires_at` with no corroboration, it archives directly -
unlike `ACTIVE`, there is no revalidation window to offer, since the fact
was never confirmed in the first place. `ACTIVE` participates in
resolution and the prompt preamble - the only state that does. `STALE` is
past its `expires_at`: dropped from the preamble but still readable by
`recall`, so an agent can revalidate it. `ARCHIVED` is retained for audit
and a history view, never read by an agent. `TOMBSTONED` is reachable
from any state - a person asking to be forgotten should not have to wait
out an expiry first - and nothing leaves it except an outright delete.

MemoryScopeType.title: MemoryScopeType
MemoryScopeType.description:
Who a memory entry belongs to, independently of which agent wrote it.

Orthogonal to `MemoryScope.agent_id`: the scope type says *whose* memory
this is, `agent_id` says whether it is confined to one agent (set) or
shared by every agent that can see that scope (`None`). The two compose
into the resolution order in `MEMORY_SCOPE_PRECEDENCE`.

`GLOBAL` deliberately has no organisation: it spans tenants, so it is
readable by every agent but never writable by one - letting an agent write
here would put one organisation's text into every other organisation's
prompts.

MemorySensitivity.title: MemorySensitivity
MemorySensitivity.description:
How exposed someone is if an entry leaks, which is what policy acts on.

Deliberately not a document-classification scale (`PUBLIC`/`INTERNAL`/...):
that answers *who may see this file*, where memory needs to know *is this
about a person, and how badly does it hurt them*. Mixing the two axes
produces values no gate can act on - a stored preference is neither public
nor internal in any sense that changes a decision.

MemoryType.title: MemoryType
MemoryType.description:
What kind of fact this is, which is what retention attaches to.

Retention belongs to the *kind* of memory, not to the store: a single
global TTL has to be either short enough to drop project context or long
enough to keep an unreliable guess, and whichever it is, it is wrong for
the other half of the data. See `MEMORY_RETENTION`.

`config` is merged into the stored config at the top level: keys present
in the body overwrite stored values, omitted keys are preserved. This
makes partial edits possible — in particular sensitive webhook keys
(`token`, `secret`), which are stripped on read and so can never be
echoed back by a client. Send an explicit `null` to clear a field. The
merge happens in `_validate_update_trigger_payload`.

existing value, or send it (a value, or `null` for "no extra args") to
replace it. The route distinguishes omitted from explicit via
`model_fields_set`; the service preserves the existing beat kwargs when
it's omitted (they aren't persisted on the row).
`response_format` behaves the same way: omit it to keep the stored format,
or send it to replace it — including an explicit `null`, which clears the
override and hands the decision back to the kind of trigger.

UsageDimension.title: UsageDimension
UsageDimension.description:
The dimension a usage aggregation groups spend by.

Backs the flagship "which agents are the most expensive?" query and its
siblings; each value maps to a column on `credit_entry_attribution`.

`EXECUTION` and `CONVERSATION` both group by a unit of work, and neither is a
subset of the other: a triggered run has an execution and charges its
wall-clock there, while a chat turn has only a conversation (see
`ChargeableMetric.CONVERSATION_TURN_TIME`). So an organisation that mostly
chats reads almost nothing under `EXECUTION`, and grouping by `CONVERSATION`
is what answers "which conversations cost us the most?".

`MODEL` groups by `credit_entry_attribution.model_identifier`, a column
added after the others (see the migration that introduced it) and
populated only going forward — there was no backfill, since the same value
already lived unindexed in `extra->>'model'` and rewriting the whole table
to promote it was judged not worth the risk for what is, at worst, a
dashboard whose `MODEL` breakdown starts partway through history. A range
that only touches rows older than the column answers "no usage", not an
error, the same way any other dimension does for a quiet period.

UsageGranularity.title: UsageGranularity
UsageGranularity.description:
The time bucket a usage time series groups spend into.

Deliberately its own enum rather than the execution domain's `UsageGrouping`:
that one offers `TOTAL`/`YEAR` (which a credit series does not) and no `WEEK`
(which it does), so reusing it would advertise members this aggregation
cannot honour.

The bucket arithmetic lives on the enum because two places need to agree on
it: the repository groups rows with the equivalent SQL `date_trunc`, and the
service reuses these methods to zero-fill the buckets that produced no spend.
Were the two to disagree, a bucket would silently vanish from the series.

the embeddings are ready the pointer flip marks it `PUBLISHED` and the
previously published version becomes `ARCHIVED`. A rollback re-publishes an
`ARCHIVED` version through the same `PUBLISHING` state. A failed go-live
returns the version to its pre-attempt state: a failed publish reverts to
`DRAFT`, a failed rollback reverts to `ARCHIVED` (see `PublishOrigin`).

Legal transitions are enforced by the `KnowledgeDocumentVersion` entity (its
status setter is a state machine); this enum only names the states. Only
`knowledge_document.published_version_id` decides what retrieval serves —
the status is descriptive history metadata for the UI.
